catalog_quote: In the phonological word one syllable bears major stress, the other syllables a lesser degree of stress. Stress always falls on one of the last three syllables, but within these three syllables its placement is unpredictable. In some cases its position is the minimal difference between a pair of words, e.g., ʔótot 'rat'; ʔotót 'flatulence'; sáʔoŋ 'adze', saʔóŋ 'canine tooth'; manbálin 'to travel', manbalín 'to become'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical/contrastive: each phonological word has one primary stress located within a three-syllable final window (antepenult, penult or ultima), its position not predictable by rule and distinguishing minimal pairs. Per Allen 1977: 283, affixable roots carry stress only on one of the last two syllables (antepenult stress is confined to a few unaffixable roots), and stress shifts one syllable rightward under suffixation for most root shapes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only that non-primary syllables bear 'a lesser degree of stress' (1975: 23); no secondary-stress rule given. Allen 1977/1980/2021 describe gemination of the onset of the pre-stress syllable when two open syllables precede the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under suffixation does not apply to roots of shape CV(C), CVC.CV, CVC.CVC (unless final vowel is e), CVC.CVC.CVC (Allen 1977: 282; 1980: 28); stress shifts left onto ma-/na-/ka- with monosyllabic stative roots; stress may not precede a root-medial consonant+glottal cluster (1977: 283). Stress correlates 'highly susceptible to higher level intonational pressures' (1975: 24). Few minimal pairs per 1975: 29, but 'many minimal pairs' per the 2021 dictionary.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, which includes enclitic pronouns (1975 sec. 1.1, e.g. ʔasáwam 'your wife', pinádasko 'I tried'). Dialect: Kibungan, Benguet (Kibungan to Bakun). Stress unmarked in practical orthography; marked with acute in the 2021 dictionary.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Lawrence Allen papers and the 2021 Webonary dictionary describe the Kankanaey of Kibungan, Benguet Province (area Kibungan north to Bakun), i.e. Central Kankanaey = Glottolog kank1243 / ISO kne, the target. Not to be confused with Northern Kankanay (Sagada; ISO xnn, Glottolog nort2877), for which Reid 1971 (data Hettick 1966) separately lists stress as phonemic, and which is probably the 'Kankanay' of Zorc's 1993 class-A list.

sources.note: Sec. 1.2 p.23: one syllable per phonological word bears major stress; stress always on one of the last three syllables but unpredictable within that window; minimal pairs ʔótot/ʔotót, sáʔoŋ/saʔóŋ, manbálin/manbalín. p.24: correlates = lengthening of peak, volume, pitch rise. Sec. 5 p.29: 'Although stress is not predictable, it is omitted from the tentative orthography...'.

sources.note: Acute accent marks the stressed vowel of polysyllables; stressed vowels louder and lengthened in open syllables; 'Many minimal pairs occur in which stress is the only distinguishing factor, e.g., ótot 'rat', otót 'flatulence'; dáan 'old', daán 'not yet'. Stress is not marked in the practical orthography.' Stress Shift rule restated.

sources.note: Sec. 2A Stress Shift pp.282-283: stress shifts one syllable right under inflectional suffixation except for roots CV(C), CVC.CV, CVC.CVC (V not e), CVC.CVC.CVC; shifts left under ma-/na-/ka- on monosyllabic statives; 'Although stress does occur on the antepenultimate syllable of a few unaffixable roots, affixable roots permit stress on one of the last two syllables only'; stress may not precede a root-medial C+glottal cluster; later: 'stress, although phonemic, is not written'.
